evidence_quotes.quote: Here we present the ﬁrst longitudinal analysis of the socio-spatial and seasonal dynamics of exposure to urban river pollution, by systematically documenting who interacts with the river and for what purpose, and how these activity patterns vary with the state water and sanitation facilities, river water quality, time of the year and sociodemographic characteristics.

We designed an interdisciplinary research approach, combining water quality monitoring, household surveys and direct observation of river use behaviour to collect empirical evidence on the state of water pollution, socio-economic proﬁles and water and sanitation challenges in riverbank settlements, and spatial and seasonal variations in people’s interactions with the river water (table 1).
A total of 1826 households were surveyed, of which 446 households were in Zone-1, 730 in Zone-2, 510 in Zone-3, and 140 in Zone-4.

Households in Zone-1 and Zone-2 access water from motorised tubewells installed by NGOs, either through pipelines drawn inside their dwelling or through shared taps in communal spaces. Those living on the southern bank of the Tongi Khal in Zone-3 have access to piped water from DWASA, whether legally or illegally, while people on the northern bank rely on community tubewells.

Although none of the households are connected to formal sewerage infrastructure, 79% households in Zone-4 use a ﬂush toilet with a septic tank and 86% do not share their toilet with others. The sanitation conditions are worst in Zone-3, with 27% reportedly using hanging latrines or practicing open defecation, with the faecal waste discharging into the river.

However, even if all these initiatives are executed effectively, the portfolio of engineering, judicial, and institutional initiatives is likely to take years to translate into reduction of pollution risks for the most vulnerable.

criterion_notes.c1: Yes (contextual/descriptive). While the primary focus is human exposure to ambient river water pollution, Section 3.2, Section 4.2, and Table 2 empirically examine household drinking water and sanitation service access across four riverbank zones in Dhaka/Gazipur to explain why low-income residents rely on polluted river water for domestic activities.
criterion_notes.c2: No under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, the study does not empirically examine any rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariffs, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, legal, institutional, and regulatory elements also are not empirically examined as explanatory factors: Section 4.2 descriptively notes that Zone-1 settlements are on private land while Zone-3 slums are on government land at risk of eviction and access DWASA piped water legally or illegally, Section 4.3 notes 60 houses evicted in an anti-encroachment drive as a reason for lower wet-season observation counts, and Sections 2.1 and 5.2 provide unanalysed background commentary on industrial effluent regulation and river-pollution policy initiatives. None of these legal or governance features are analysed empirically in relation to water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Contains primary empirical data combining 12 months of river water quality monitoring (13 points), heavy metal and biotoxicity analysis (22 points), a cross-sectional survey of 1,826 riverbank households, and 7,900 structured direct observations of river use across dry and wet seasons.
criterion_notes.c4: Yes (descriptive WASH metrics alongside primary river-exposure outcomes). Section 4.2 and Table 2 report household drinking water source (piped into dwelling/yard vs. motorised tubewell), water point sharing, restricted hours of supply/queues, sanitation facility type (flush to septic tank, improved/unimproved pit latrine, hanging toilet/open defecation), and toilet sharing across the four study zones, while the main analytical outcome is direct human contact with polluted river water.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Population and units of analysis (1,826 surveyed households and 7,900 river-use observations across 852 three-hour observation slots), exposures (spatial/seasonal river pollution, sociodemographic status, and local WASH deprivation), outcomes (river-use behaviours and descriptive household WASH indicators), and mixed observational/survey study design are clearly reported.

study_design: Interdisciplinary observational study combining longitudinal river water quality monitoring (12 months), heavy metal and biotoxicity testing, a cross-sectional household survey (n = 1,826), and two-season structured direct observation of river-use behaviour (7,900 observations over 33 days).
population_and_sample: Riverbank communities and river users along a 25 km stretch of the Turag River and Tongi Khal in Dhaka and Gazipur districts, Bangladesh: 1,826 surveyed households across four zones (Zone-1: 446; Zone-2: 730; Zone-3: 510; Zone-4: 140), 7,900 structured direct observations of river use across 852 three-hour slots over 33 days at 10 observation points (grouped into 6 sites), and monthly/seasonal river water samples at 13 to 22 sampling points.
exposure: Spatial and seasonal variations in ambient river water pollution (physiochemical parameters, pathogens, heavy metals, biotoxicity, Bishwa Ijtema gathering) and household socio-economic status and local WASH conditions across four riverbank zones (no legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism empirically examined).
outcome: Primary outcome: gender-, age-, spatial-, and season-disaggregated direct human interaction with polluted river water (dishwashing, laundry, bathing, swimming, fishing, boating, hanging latrine use/open defecation). Descriptive/contextual WASH metrics: household drinking water source, water source sharing, intermittent supply hours, sanitation facility type, and toilet sharing.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the study collects primary empirical survey data on household water and sanitation conditions across four riverbank zones in Dhaka/Gazipur (Table 2, Section 4.2), WASH deprivation is examined as a socio-spatial contextual driver of direct human contact with polluted river water rather than as an outcome of any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance mechanism. Land tenure (private vs. government land), legal/illegal DWASA connections, river-encroachment evictions, and environmental regulations appear only as unanalysed background description or narrative policy commentary (Sections 2.1, 4.2, 4.3, and 5.2), failing Criterion 2 under both the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope and the plain wording.
